notes: Every row's token spelling and purpose comes from the operator's own documentation, linked in `docs`, read on the date in `verified`.

`purpose` is the field most lists leave out and the one that changes the decision: `train` is a corpus for a future model, `answer` is a fetch made while a person waits for an answer that can cite and link you, `search` builds an index, `ads` checks ad landing pages, `preview` builds a link preview, and `agent` is a browser an assistant drives on one person’s behalf — a visitor, not a crawler.

`crawls: false` marks a control-only robots.txt token that fetches nothing by itself (Google-Extended, Applebot-Extended). Disallowing it changes how already-crawled content may be used; it does not remove you from search.
`respects_robots: false` marks an agent whose own operator documents that it may ignore robots.txt. For those, a robots.txt verdict states your request, not an outcome.

`signed_requests: web-bot-auth` appears only where the operator's own page says its requests are cryptographically signed under Web Bot Auth (RFC 9421), so a site can verify the crawler by signature instead of trusting the user agent. Absent means the page does not say, not that the crawler does not sign.

crawlers.note: Checks the safety of landing pages submitted as adverts in ChatGPT. OpenAI documents that it visits only those submitted pages and that its data does not train their foundation models.

A browser hosted by Anthropic and driven by an agent at one user’s direction, which Anthropic documents separately from its crawlers and fetchers. It carries the browser’s own User-Agent with the token added inside it, so a rule has to match the token rather than the whole string, and Anthropic publishes the addresses it comes from at claude.com/.well-known/sail under the same name. Anthropic states that a site’s preferences for its crawlers and for this traffic are independent of each other, and does not describe this traffic as governed by robots.txt.

A robots.txt token with no user-agent string of its own. It controls whether crawled content may train future Gemini models and ground answers in Gemini Apps and Vertex AI. Google documents that it does not affect inclusion in Google Search and is not a ranking signal.
A generic crawler any Google product team may use, including one-off research crawls. Google documents that rules for it affect no specific product.
Not an AI crawler. It is in the dataset because AI Overviews are built from the Google index, so blocking it removes a site from both.

Google documents that rules addressed to this token affect only crawls that a site owner has asked for when building a Vertex AI agent, and have no effect on Google Search or any other product. So it is the one row here that a site usually meets because somebody on that site asked for it.

Google documents this as the identity used by agents hosted on Google infrastructure to navigate the web and perform actions upon user request. It is listed among the user-triggered fetchers, and that page states that because the fetch was requested by a user, these fetchers generally ignore robots.txt rules — so a Disallow written for it describes the site’s request rather than the traffic. Google governs it by publishing the addresses it comes from, in user-triggered-agents.json, and is also experimenting with the Web Bot Auth protocol under the identity agent.bot.goog.

Fetches the individual URLs a Gemini Notebook user has given as sources for their own project, so it arrives because a reader chose that page, one URL at a time, and not as a crawl. It is a user-triggered fetcher, which Google documents as generally ignoring robots.txt. The token read Google-NotebookLM until that spelling stopped being supported in August 2026; a rule still naming the old one matches nothing today.
Perplexity's own documentation states that because the fetch is user-initiated it generally ignores robots.txt rules.

Powers Spotlight, Siri and Safari search, and Apple documents that what it crawls may also train their foundation models. Where robots.txt names Googlebot but not Applebot, Apple documents that Applebot follows the Googlebot rules.
Controls whether what Applebot already crawled may train Apple’s foundation models. Apple documents that it crawls no pages and that disallowing it does not remove pages from search results.
Crawls for Meta AI search results, which Meta documents as citing and linking the content.
Meta documents that it may bypass robots.txt because it fetches single links at a user’s request.
Builds the title, description and thumbnail of a link shared in Meta apps. Meta documents that it may bypass robots.txt for security and integrity checks.

Amazon documents it as improving its products and services, and states that what it collects may be used to train Amazon AI models — which is why it sits in the training group now that Amazon documents a separate token for each of the other two jobs. It honours the user-agent and allow/disallow directives, may act on a robots.txt copy cached for up to 30 days, respects rel=nofollow and the noarchive, noindex and none meta tags, and does not support crawl-delay.

Allowing it makes a site eligible to appear in Amazon search experiences such as Alexa, and Amazon states that it does not crawl content for generative AI model training — so a site that blocked everything Amazon in order to stay out of a model gave up the visitors too. Where robots.txt names no group for it but allows other search bots, Amazon documents that it follows the directives given to those.

The fetch Amazon makes while a person waits — it brings live information from the web to answer an Alexa question on that user’s behalf. Amazon states that because the action can be initiated by a user it may not follow all robots.txt directives, and that it does not crawl content for generative AI model training.

The crawler an Amazon Q Business customer points at websites to index them for their own assistant, so a site usually meets it because somebody using that site configured it. AWS documents that it adheres to robots.txt and respects Allow and Disallow, and writes the token in lower case in its own examples. The same page states that Q Business is no longer open to new customers.
Not an AI crawler. It is in the dataset because Copilot answers are built on the Bing index.
Builds the public Common Crawl corpus that many model builders then use. Disallowing it is not retroactive: it does not remove a site from archives already published.

Diffbot documents this as general, proactive crawling that builds a search index and its Knowledge Graph, so that sites can be discovered and cited in response to keyword queries, and states that it is not used for AI training. It adds that Diffbot does not crawl pages for training generative foundation models at all. By default its crawls adhere to robots.txt, including disallow and crawl-delay, though Diffbot says the file can be overridden where a partnership or agreement with the site exists.

Requests made on behalf of a person browsing a URL with Diffbot software, in response to their input. The robots.txt statement on Diffbot’s page is written about its crawls and promises nothing for this token, which is why this row states no commitment. The page also separates Diffbot’s Extract and Crawlbot APIs, where customers define their own crawl and carry their own user agent, from these two tokens.

Collects publicly available images for Hive’s web-intelligence products, which is why it sits in the training group rather than beside the crawlers that answer a question. The operator page commits in writing to robots.txt directives that name ImagesiftBot and to the crawl-delay directive, read as the minimum seconds between requests. The page also spells the name ImageSiftBot in prose; the token it actually sends, and the one its own robots.txt examples use, is ImagesiftBot, and a rule has to match that spelling.

Haiku’s indexing robot for institutional public data, mainly court decisions and legal documents under Open Data standards. Haiku states that it is not used to explore content in order to train its generative AI base models, that data likely to change is collected on a sliding window not exceeding ninety days, and that a site can exclude it by naming the token in a User-agent line.

The robot used for a direct request from a Haiku user. Haiku states that it is not used to explore the web automatically nor for generative AI training, that it does not record information from third-party sites when a request comes from a user, and that its search follows a whitelist policy and is not a general search engine. It recommends that a site wanting to appear in those results authorise Haiku-SearchBot in robots.txt. Haiku also documents that it subcontracts some web search to Google, and relies on the Googlebot rules for that path.

Builds and maintains the search index behind Parallel’s web APIs, and Parallel notes that restricting it reduces a site’s visibility through them. It follows the group naming ShapBot, or the * group when none does, reflects robots.txt changes within about a day, honours crawl-delay, and pauses on a 429 or 503 carrying Retry-After. It signs its requests under Web Bot Auth, with keys published at shapbot.parallel.ai.

Identifies itself when Parallel retrieves content at a user’s direction, and is not used to crawl the web automatically. Parallel states that it is intended to provide visibility to content owners rather than to be managed through automated controls, and sends anyone who wants to control automated crawling to ShapBot instead — so a robots.txt rule for this token is a statement of preference, and Parallel does not promise to act on it. Its requests are signed under Web Bot Auth, with keys at shap-user.parallel.ai.

An agent that browses on behalf of a signed-in Hark user, for research, form-filling and account actions on services that user already has access to, one request per tool invocation. Hark states that it is not a search crawler and does not index the web, build datasets or train models on what it fetches. Its page never mentions robots.txt: the controls it offers are signed requests (Web Bot Auth, Ed25519), published IP ranges, a listing in Cloudflare’s verified-bot directory, and a way to ask for a blocklist entry, so this row states no robots.txt commitment.

The fetch made when somebody asks Kimi to read a page or answer something that needs live retrieval. Moonshot states that it is not used for bulk crawling and that, because the actions are user-triggered, robots.txt rules may not directly apply — and separately that disallowing it may reduce a site’s visibility in user-directed searches through its products. Moonshot also asks sites not to block its IP ranges, because a blocked crawler cannot read the robots.txt that states the site’s preferences.

Builds the index that Exa search and the applications on top of it answer from, and Exa states that it sends people back to the source. Its robots.txt precedence is unusual and worth knowing: with no group naming ExaSearchBot it follows the rules set for major search engines, and only then the * group. Exa also documents that robots.txt governs crawling and not indexing — a page already in the index leaves it on a noindex meta tag or X-Robots-Tag header, at the next re-fetch — and that every request is signed under Web Bot Auth (RFC 9421), with Ed25519 keys published at crawler.exa.ai, so the user agent alone should not be trusted.
The same crawler fetching images, under its own token, so a site can keep its pages in the index and keep its images out of it.

The pages Exa fetches on one user’s request rather than by crawling. Exa’s page names the token and separates it from the crawler, but its robots.txt section is written about ExaSearchBot alone and promises nothing for this one, which is why this row states no commitment rather than borrowing the crawler’s.

Builds and refreshes Liner’s search and reference index, including paper metadata, citations and DOI resolution. Liner documents that each of its two bots follows the group naming its own token and the * group otherwise, and that rules for this one do not apply to the other. Liner states that both of its bots sign their requests under Web Bot Auth.

Fetches a page in real time when a Liner user asks a question, and the answer cites that page as its source. Unlike the fetchers whose operators lean on the fetch being user-initiated to say robots.txt may not apply — Perplexity-User, Meta-ExternalFetcher, Kimi-User, ExaUser, Amzn-User and Google’s user-triggered fetchers — Liner commits to the file anyway: it documents that this bot follows the group naming Liner-User, and the * group when none does. Both Liner bots sign their requests under Web Bot Auth with separate keys, and Liner states it publishes no IP ranges, so the signature is the only verification offered.

Collects publicly available content that may train ElevenLabs’ generative models. ElevenLabs documents that the two tokens are independent of each other, so a site can allow the one its customers use while disallowing this one, and that a robots.txt change is reflected within about 24 hours.

Fetches the pages an ElevenLabs customer adds to an agent’s knowledge base, when they add them and when they refresh them, and ElevenLabs states that it honours robots.txt. Like Google’s Vertex crawler, a site usually meets it because somebody using that site asked for it.

Qualified documents that it crawls its own customers’ websites to power its AI products, at setup, at major releases and on a schedule the customer sets with their account manager. Its page never mentions robots.txt: the only crawl control it offers is to contact that manager, which is why this row states no robots.txt commitment rather than inferring one. It also documents that it may present a modified Chromium user agent with the token inside it, so a rule has to match the token and not the whole string.

candidates_awaiting_a_reference.why_here: Widely seen in access logs and widely reported to ignore robots.txt. Re-checked on 2026-11-21: ByteDance still publishes no page naming the token.
Seen in logs and in other lists. Re-checked on 2026-11-21: Cohere still publishes no page naming the token.
No operator documentation found, re-checked on 2026-11-21.
Re-checked on 2026-11-21: webz.io answers 403 to our requests, so we can neither read a page naming the token nor state that none exists. Either way there is nothing cited to promote this row on.
